passages.original: 2. Ad Augustinum quod attinet, finitam dixit causam, quatenus aperte ac certa auctoritate crant reprobati errores; at finitam noa intellexit, quate- nus istud fixam sonat ac determinatam etiam per- sonarum Pelagii ac Coelestii condemnationem.
passages.english: 2. As for Augustine, he said the case was finished insofar as the errors had been condemned openly and by sure authority; but he did not understand it as finished insofar as that would signify a fixed and settled condemnation of the persons of Pelagius and Caelestius as well.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: 'crant' read as 'erant', 'noa' as 'non'.

passages.original: 4. AEgrius percipitur, quo pacto probari potuerit fides Coelestii, qui, Augustino teste (Ibid. c. 33), « in libello suo, quem Romae gestis ecclesiasticis allegavit, parvulos et baptizari in remissionem pec- catorum confessus est, et negavit ullum habere ori- ginale peccatum. » Ipsa autem hujus haeretici verba idem Doctor refert lib. de Pecc. orig. c. 6. Zosimum tamen variis modis excusant tum Marius Mercator, ut jam vidimus, tum Augustinus ipse, ut nunc paucis exponendum.
passages.english: 4. It is harder to grasp how the faith of Caelestius could have been approved, since, as Augustine testifies (ibid., ch. 33), "in his booklet, which he submitted at Rome to the ecclesiastical proceedings, he both confessed that little children are baptized for the remission of sins and denied that they have any original sin." The same Doctor reports the very words of this heretic in the book On Original Sin, ch. 6. Yet Zosimus is excused in various ways both by Marius Mercator, as we have already seen, and by Augustine himself, as must now be set out briefly.

passages.original: sic fovere, ut « inter- posito duorum mensium tempore, donec rescribere- tur ex Africa, resipiscendi ei locus » concederetur. Interea « et hoc (scil. peccatum originale a Coelestio non negari) ut plenius et manifestius in illo fieret, exspectabatur, venturis ex Africa litteris, in qua provincia ejus aliquanto calliditas evidentius inno- tuerat » (Lib. iiad Bonifac., c, 3). Tum igitur, ut verbis utamur Augustini, « voluntas emendationis, non falsitas dogmatis approbata est. » Quamobrem apposite idem concludit Augustinus : Profecto quid- quid interea lenius actum est cum Coelestio, servata dumtaxat antiquissimae et robustissimae fidei firmi- tate, correctionis fuit clementissima suasio, non ap- probatio exitiosissima pravitatis. Et quod ab codem sacerdote (Zosimo) postea Coelestius et Pelagius repe- tita auctoritate damnati sunt, paululum intermissae, jam necessario proferendae severitatis fuit, non prae- varicatio prius cognitae, vel nova cognitio veritatis.
passages.english: to cherish [him] in such a way that, "with an interval of two months set, until a reply should be written from Africa, room for coming to his senses" might be granted him. Meanwhile "this too (namely, that original sin was not denied by Caelestius) was awaited, so that it might be made more fully and more clearly evident in him, when letters should come from Africa, the province in which his cunning had become known somewhat more plainly" (Book 2 to Boniface, ch. 3). At that time, then, to use Augustine's words, "it was the will to amend that was approved, not the falsity of the doctrine." Therefore the same Augustine aptly concludes: Certainly, whatever was done more leniently with Caelestius in the meantime, provided only that the firmness of the most ancient and most robust faith was preserved, was a most merciful persuasion toward correction, not a most ruinous approval of depravity. And that Caelestius and Pelagius were afterwards condemned by the same priest (Zosimus) with renewed authority was a matter of a severity briefly suspended and now necessarily to be brought forth, not a betrayal of a truth previously known, nor a new knowledge of the truth.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence. 'iiad' read as 'ii ad'; 'codem' as 'eodem'.

passages.original: 278), fatetur tamen non secus de illo sentiendum esse, ac de Atha- nasio cum Timotheum Apollinaris discipulum Da- maso commendavit, de ipso Damaso cum commen- datum benigne suscepit, ac de Palaestinis episcopis cum Pelagium orthodoxum judicarunt; « quoniam, inquit, non debet crimini deputari simplicium, non intellecta versutia malignorum. » Et ea quidem crat versutia, ut ex Pelagii litteris tunc Zosimo datis hunc haereticum credidisset Augustinus plane correctam nisi varias illius artes aliunde compertas habuisset, mi fidem faciunt ipsius Augustini verba notis in epi- stolam 42 Pelagii, ad Innocentium, pag.
passages.english: 278), nevertheless admits that one must judge of him no differently than of Athanasius when he commended Timothy, the disciple of Apollinaris, to Damasus; of Damasus himself when he kindly received the man so commended; and of the bishops of Palestine when they judged Pelagius orthodox; "since," he says, "the cunning of the malicious, not understood, ought not to be counted as a crime of the simple." And indeed such was the cunning that Augustine would have believed, from the letters of Pelagius then given to Zosimus, that this heretic had been plainly corrected, had he not learned of his various artifices from other sources. Of this the words of Augustine himself convince me, cited in the notes on letter 42, of Pelagius to Innocent, page
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: "crat" read as "erat"; "mi" read as "mihi"; "correctam" taken as "correctum" (agreeing with "hunc haereticum"). The sentence continues into the following context ("918, n. g"), so the page reference is incomplete here.

passages.original: Tametsi enim, etiam postquam ab episcopatu remoti sunt, a Mario Mercatore studiosi episcopi; a concilio Car- thaginiensi epist. 26, ad Innocentium, n. i, sancti fratres et consacerdotes; ab Augustino lib. de Gestis Pelagii c. i, item sancti fratres et coepiscopi nostri Galli nuncupentur; longe tamen aliud de illis Zosi- mus sibi referri audiebat. In epistola nempe Pelagii legebat, teste Augustino ( Lib. de Gratia Chr. c. 33), ipsius Pelagii « invidiosas de inimicis suis querelas, » quae maxime in eos cadebant. Neque iis dubio pro- cul parcebat Praylii Hierosolymitani antistitis « eni- xius Pelagii causae intervenientis » epistola.
passages.english: For although, even after they had been removed from the episcopate, they are called "zealous bishops" by Marius Mercator, "holy brothers and fellow priests" by the Council of Carthage (letter 26, to Innocent, n. 1), and likewise "holy brothers and our fellow bishops of Gaul" by Augustine (On the Proceedings of Pelagius, ch. 1), Zosimus nevertheless heard something very different reported to him about them. Namely, in the letter of Pelagius he read, as Augustine testifies (On the Grace of Christ, ch. 33), Pelagius' own "spiteful complaints about his enemies," which fell chiefly upon them. Nor, without doubt, did the letter of Praylius, bishop of Jerusalem, who "intervened very earnestly on behalf of Pelagius' cause," spare them.

passages.original: » E re autem Patrocli erat, ut Heros, in cujus locum invaserat, existimatione damnatus esset. Quidquid igitur Zosimus in epistolis suis ad- versus Herotem scripsit, ex illius fide non immerito creditur dixisse. Patroclus autem, ut Prosper in Chronico docet, tam perditae conscientiae erat, ut « infami mercatu » sacerdotia venditare non dubitaret. Quod dum ignorat Zosimus, ex ore trium testium de Lazaro et Herote inter se consentientium, aequum de illis judicium proferre se existimavit.
passages.english: " It was moreover in Patroclus' interest that Heros, into whose place he had intruded, should be condemned in reputation. Whatever, therefore, Zosimus wrote against Heros in his letters is not without reason believed to have been said on the strength of that man's word. Patroclus, however, as Prosper teaches in his Chronicle, was of so depraved a conscience that he did not hesitate to sell priestly offices "in infamous traffic." Being unaware of this, Zosimus thought that, on the testimony of three witnesses agreeing among themselves about Lazarus and Heros, he was pronouncing a fair judgement on them.
passages.notes: The opening quotation mark closes a quotation from Prosper begun in the preceding context.
